en: One fascicle of the *Record of Aids to the Laṅkāvatāra*,
compiled by the Śramaṇa Shi Jingjue of the Eastern Capital while residing at Lingquan Valley on Mount Taihang.
First: Saṃghavarman,
Tripiṭaka Master of the Song Dynasty,
a native of Central India.
When he was studying the Mahāyāna, he was known as Mahāyan.
During the Yuanjia era,
he traveled by ship to Guangzhou.
Emperor Taizu of the Song dynasty welcomed him at Danyang Commandery,
where he translated the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra.
King Wen invited both monastics and laypeople to request that he expound upon the instructions of Chan.
Because Buddhabhadra was not yet proficient in the Song language, he felt ashamed;
consequently, he frequently dreamed of people offering him their heads in exchange for his own with a sword.
Thereupon, he opened the instructions for meditation. The Tripiṭaka Master said:
"In this land, the earth lies toward the eastern side."
The path of cultivation lacks fixed dharmas;
because it lacks fixed dharmas,
one may fall into the vehicles of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas.
Or they may fall into the ninety-five kinds of heterodox teachings,
or fall into the meditative absorption of ghosts and spirits,
wherein they perceive all things as objects of contemplation.
To know the good and evil affairs of others' households—
how bitter! Great fortune and great calamity.
Falling into ruin themselves and causing others to fall as well— I pity these people,
who for long eons shall descend into the realm of ghosts and spirits.
Having long endured birth and death,
they fail to attain liberation;
some even fall into the ways of sorcery.
They employ ghosts and spirits to observe the good and evil affairs of others;
who says that I am practicing seated meditation and contemplative cultivation?
Ordinary beings, blinded by ignorance and lacking understanding,
claim that upon ascending the Path of the Sages,
all [afflictions] are completely subdued.
"You do not know that this is the dharma of ghosts, spirits, and malevolent demons.
In our Central Kingdom, there is the True Dharma;
it is kept secret and not transmitted in writing."
There are those whose roots of merit have matured who,
encountering a virtuous and wise person on the road,
receive [the teaching] while on their journey.
If one does not encounter a virtuous and wise person,
father and son cannot attain [realization].
The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says:
The mind of all Buddhas is supreme.
When teaching the Dharma,
it is precisely this state where the mind does not arise.
This Dharma transcends the three vehicles and surpasses the ten stages,
reaching the ultimate state of Buddhahood.
One can only know this within one's own silent mind:
by being without mind, one nourishes the spirit;
by being without thought, one brings peace to the body.
Dwelling in seclusion and sitting in purity,
one guards the fundamental and returns to the truth;
the Dharma of mine is profound and silent.
It is not something transmitted by ordinary people of shallow understanding;
it must be those with profound merit who are able to receive and practice it.
If one does not understand the point,

if one understands the point...
In the eighth [stage], there is no sixth or seventh;
those who intend to become Buddhas first study the settling of the mind (anxin).
When the mind is not yet at peace,
even the good is not truly good;
how much more so the evil!
When the mind attains tranquility, both good and evil have no basis. As the Avataṃsaka Sūtra says:
"Phenomenon and phenomenon do not know one another."
Having come to this country,
I have yet to see even a single person practicing the Way,
let alone one who has attained peace of mind.

or which are pursued for the sake of fame.
It becomes a source of gain;

What is envy? It is to see another person practicing the Way,
attaining both principle and practice.
When many people take refuge [in them] and offer worship,
they immediately give rise to a mind of jealousy and a mind of hatred and disdain.
To rely on one's own cleverness and refuse to accept those who surpass oneself is called envy.
With this wisdom and understanding,

One cannot attain tranquility;

If that were so, even if one practices the six pāramitās,
lectures on the sūtras, dwells in the second or third dhyānas,

This is called "practice according to the Dharma. Now, regarding what is termed "settling the mind," there are briefly four types.
The first is the mind that turns its back on principle.
The first refers to the mind of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) who is entirely unenlightened.
The second is the mind directed toward principle (*tattva*),
which refers to the state of revulsion toward birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
Seeking nirvana and tending toward tranquility—
this is called the mind of a śrāvaka.
Third is the mind that enters into principle (*nyāya*).
This means that although one has severed the hindrances and manifested the principle,
the subject and object have not yet been eliminated.
This is the mind of the bodhisattva.
Fourth is the mind of principle,
which means that there is no principle external to non-principle.
It is not a mind external to the mind;
its principle is precisely the mind.
The mind is capable of equanimity.
That which is named "principle" (li) is that which illuminates and is capable of clarity;
that which is named "mind" (xin) is this very illumination.
Psychological equanimity is called the Buddha-mind;
it is that which realizes the true nature.
One does not perceive any distinction between birth-and-death and nirvana,
nor any difference between the ordinary person and the sage;
object and wisdom are non-dual.
Principle and phenomena are both fused;
the ultimate and the conventional are viewed as equal;
defilement and purity are one and the same.
The Buddha and sentient beings are fundamentally equal and of one and the same limit.
As the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra says:
There is no nirvana for anything whatsoever;
there is no Buddha who has attained nirvana,
nor is there a nirvana belonging to a Buddha.
One remains far removed from both the awakening and that which is awakened;
whether it be existence or non-existence,
one is entirely free from both.
The Great Way is fundamentally vast and pervasive;
it is perfectly pure and primordially present,
not obtained through causes.
It is like sunlight beneath floating clouds;
when the clouds and mist are completely extinguished,
the sunlight manifests of its own accord.
What use is it to extensively study and acquire knowledge and views,
or to traverse the realms of written characters and spoken language,
only to return once more to the path of birth and death?

The marvelous, tranquil,

Supremely vast and expansive,

Why is this? Because bats,
owls, and horn-owls perceive darkness as light when they see it.
Ordinary people perceive the light of others as darkness;
all such views are merely false conceptualizations.
Because of their inverted views and because of karmic obstructions,
they do not perceive the true Dharma.

his divine wisdom was profound and clear.
Upon hearing this, he attained full understanding;
his resolve was set upon the Mahāyāna path,
and thus he abandoned the white robes for the black.
He brought the holy teachings to flourishing prosperity; his mind was darkly attuned to emptiness and stillness,
and he possessed penetrating insight into worldly affairs.
Illuminating both within and without,
his virtue transcends the mundane world;
he feels compassion and regret for those in remote regions.
As the true teaching declined and fell into disuse,
he was thus able to travel far across mountains and seas to wander and transform the lands of Han and Wei.

The paths for entering the Way are many;
to summarize them,
they do not exceed two kinds.
The first is entry through principle;
the second is entry through practice.
As for entry through principle:
This means relying on the teachings to awaken to the fundamental principle.
One must have deep faith that all living beings,
whether ordinary or sagely, share the same true nature.
It is merely because it is obscured by adventitious delusions that it cannot be clearly manifested.
If one abandons delusion and returns to the truth, [it will be revealed].
Abiding in concentrated contemplation,

Firmly abiding without wavering,
one no longer follows verbal instructions;
this is precisely to be in profound accord with ultimate truth.
There is no conceptual discrimination;
it is the entry into the principle of quiescent namelessness.
As for the "entry by practice":
These are called the four practices;
all other practices are entirely included within these.
What are the four modes of conduct?
First, returning enmity;
second, acting in accordance with conditions.
Third is the practice of seeking nothing;
fourth is the practice in accordance with the Dharma.
What is the practice of requiting resentment?

Why is this? Because consciousness penetrates the fundamental source.
When this mind arises, [it is so].
It accords with principle;

It is said that this is the practice of repaying enmity.
Second, as for the practitioner who acts in accordance with conditions:
sentient beings have no self.
Furthermore, transmitted by karma,

If one obtains superior rewards such as honor and fame,

When conditions are exhausted, one returns to non-existence; what cause for joy is there?
Gain and loss follow from conditions.
The mind is without increase or decrease;

Therefore, it is said that one acts in accordance with conditions;

The people of the world are long lost in delusion;
